questions.q: Why does the minimum-variance portfolio's weight formula require no expected-return estimates, while the tangency portfolio's formula does?
options: Both formulas actually require expected returns; the lesson's min-variance example is incomplete
Expected returns are never actually used in real portfolio optimization
Minimum-variance only minimizes risk (a function of the covariance matrix alone); the tangency portfolio maximizes risk-adjusted RETURN, which inherently requires expected returns as an input
The tangency portfolio formula uses only the covariance matrix, identical to min-variance
questions.explain: Min-variance asks only 'what's the lowest-risk combination,' answerable purely from covariances; tangency asks 'what's the best risk-adjusted return,' which inherently needs a return estimate.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is the min-variance portfolio's volatility (12.95%) LOWER than even the least volatile individual asset (15%)?
options: The least volatile asset was excluded entirely from the min-variance portfolio
This result indicates a calculation error, since a portfolio should never be less volatile than its least volatile component
Diversification -- combining imperfectly-correlated assets can produce a portfolio safer than any single holding, purely from the covariance structure
Diversification only reduces volatility when correlations are negative
questions.explain: This is diversification working exactly as intended -- even with positive correlations, combining assets that aren't perfectly correlated can reduce overall portfolio volatility below any single component's own volatility.

options: A theoretical concept with no practical application to actual portfolio construction
The minimum-variance portfolio specifically, with no other points on the curve
A single optimal portfolio that is correct for every investor regardless of risk tolerance
The full curve of portfolios delivering the maximum possible return for every achievable level of risk -- not a single point
questions.explain: The frontier is a curve, not a point -- every portfolio on it is optimal for its own specific risk level, and where to sit on that curve is a separate risk-tolerance question.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Lesson 25's covariance shrinkage work matters even more in this specific lesson?
options: Shrinkage only matters for factor models, never for portfolio optimization
Both the min-variance and tangency formulas require INVERTING the covariance matrix, and a poorly-conditioned or singular raw sample covariance matrix makes that inversion numerically unstable
This lesson avoids matrix inversion entirely, making shrinkage irrelevant
Shrinkage is unrelated to anything covered in this lesson
questions.explain: Matrix inversion is the specific operation that makes an ill-conditioned covariance matrix a real practical problem, not just a statistical nicety -- shrinkage directly protects this lesson's computation from producing unstable, nonsensical weights.

questions.q: What is the classic symptom of optimizing a portfolio on an ill-conditioned (poorly estimated) covariance matrix?
options: A portfolio that always perfectly matches the equal-weight benchmark
Extreme long/short positions that flip entirely with tiny changes in the input data
Weights that are always exactly equal across all assets
A minimum-variance portfolio with a volatility higher than any individual asset
questions.explain: Instability -- wildly different weights from small input changes -- is the characteristic symptom of inverting a poorly-conditioned covariance matrix, which is exactly why shrinkage (Lesson 25) matters before running this optimization.
